newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean union abandons one-day strikes.
newsitem.headline: South Korean union abandons one-day strikes.

text.p: South Korea's outlawed union said on Tuesday it was abandoning its one-day-a-week strikes, partly due to economic turmoil caused by the collapse of the country's second largest steelmaker.
But the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions still plans full stoppages starting on February 18 unless the government scraps a controversial new labour law.
The confederation led almost four weeks of intermittent wildcat strikes after the law was rammed through parliament on December 26.

It ordered its 500,000 members to walk out on Wednesdays only after President Kim Young-sam agreed to return the bill to parliament for debate, and lifted the threat of arrest against its leaders sheltering in a Seoul cathedral.
However, Kim has rejected union demands to scrap the legislation, which makes it easier for companies to lay off workers and hire temporary staff.
"We have postponed Wednesday strikes to prepare for the fourth stage of strikes on Febuary 18," said confederation official Chung Sung-hee.
"We also took into consideration economic difficulties faced by the country as a result of the Hanbo incident."
Banks and financial markets have been battered by the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co under a mountain of debts worth $5.8 billion.
On Tuesday, Hanbo Steel sought court protection along with another affiliate of the Hanbo Group, the country's 14th largest industrial conglomerate, or "chaebol".
Confederation president Kwon Young-kil warned the government against trying to manipulate the Hanbo crisis.
"If the government tries to use the Hanbo incident to divert attention away from the labour law issue we will start full strikes immediately," he told reporters.

"The Hanbo incident shows how wrong the government and chaebols are to try to strengthen the nation's economy through an evil law that allows layoffs, part-time staffing and replacements of strikers."
"We ask the government to thoroughly investigate the Hanbo incident and prosecute everyone involved," Kwon said.
He said in place of strikes on Wednesdays the union would organise rallies.

Meanwhile, Hyundai Motor Co, South Korea's largest car maker, said it was delaying salary payments to 20,000 office staff because it was short of cash after the strikes, which hit the auto industry hardest.
It was the first time the company has failed to pay workers on time since 1979, company official Shin Dong-woo said.
The company estimates production losses at its main factory in Ulsan at 670 billion won ($784 million).
"The strikes dragged on for longer than expected and during that time the company was not able to raise money from sales so it is short of working capital," Shin said.
Hyundai was having trouble securing bank loans because of tight liquidity in the banking system following the collapse of Hanbo Steel, he added.
Blue-collar workers would not be affected by the salary delay. Office workers had been told they will be paid in full before the start of the lunar New Year holiday on Febuary 7, Shin said.
On Saturday, Ulsan production line workers worked a full day instead of a usual half day, and they also worked through the Sunday holiday to try to make up losses.
